kurz: Why even ten years of outperformance is almost never enough to distinguish skill from luck statistically.

bloecke.md: After five years, two fund managers are ten percentage points apart. Before anyone can say who was better, it has to be established whether the difference means anything at all. Every investment result is made up of the decision-maker's skill and of what simply came their way, and the two parts cannot be separated by looking at the result itself. Statistics can only offer a cross-check for this. It states how likely such a result would be even without any skill at all.

## The scale between skill and chance

Michael Mauboussin arranges activities on an axis between two poles. At one end is chess, with no dice and no hidden cards. The stronger player almost always wins, and just a few games reveal the ranking. At the other end is roulette, where even many repetitions bring no clarity. Active investing lies closer to the roulette end. Skill exists there, but the element of chance in each observation drowns out the signal.

Mauboussin's test is the question of whether you can lose on purpose. At the roulette table you cannot, because every way of betting has the same expected value. In a portfolio you certainly can, for example through expensive purchases, frequent trading and high fees. That is why skill exists in the markets. It just cannot be read off where most people look for it, namely in the league table of the last three years.

That skill exists is undisputed. The only open question is whether a particular track record is long and clear enough to distinguish it from luck. This second question is not a matter of opinion; it can be answered by calculation.

## The paradox of skill

The better all participants become, the more chance decides. This seems contradictory, but it follows necessarily from the fact that the observed dispersion of results is made up of the dispersion of skill and the dispersion of chance. If the level of all participants rises and becomes more uniform, the first component becomes smaller while the second stays the same. The gap between first place and fiftieth place therefore depends more and more on luck.

The standard example comes from baseball. Since Ted Williams in 1941, no player has reached a batting average of .400, even though athletes and training are far better today. The talent is still there; what has become smaller is the spread between the players. The same process took place in the fund industry. The lead of good managers over average ones has shrunk, while the random fluctuations of the markets have stayed the same.

bloecke.titel: Years needed for statistically proven outperformance (t = 2)
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation using Years = (2 × Tracking error ÷ Outperformance)². Almost all combinations that occur in practice lie in the dark cells.

bloecke.md:
A manager with a calm style and one point of excess return would need a hundred years with a 5% tracking error. In technical terms, the ratio of outperformance to tracking error is called the [[Information ratio|information ratio]], and t is the information ratio times the square root of the years. An information ratio of 0.5 is considered very good and needs 16 years to reach t = 2.

In addition, the typical outperformance is not positive at all. For European retail funds over the ten years to 2021, ESMA found net returns of 9.4% a year for active equity funds and 10.6% for passive ones, with costs of 1.50% and 0.53%. The return difference of 1.2 points is of the same order of magnitude as the cost difference of 0.97 points. If the outperformance is negative, any significance calculation becomes unnecessary.

From 1964 to 2014, Berkshire Hathaway increased its book value per share by 19.4% a year, while the S&P 500 including dividends rose by 9.9%. That is around 9.5 points of outperformance over 50 years (shareholder letter 2014). For this concentrated portfolio, a high tracking error of 15 percentage points is assumed.

- After 5 years, t = (9.5 ÷ 15) × 2.24 = 1.4 (not significant).
- After 10 years, t = (9.5 ÷ 15) × 3.16 = 2.0 (just at the threshold).
- After 50 years, t = (9.5 ÷ 15) × 7.07 = 4.5 (clearly significant).

Even this outperformance, which practically nobody has repeated since 1964, was not statistically meaningful after five years. A league table covering three years is therefore even less suitable as evidence of skill.

## Buffett's superinvestors

In 1984, Warren Buffett gave a talk at Columbia Business School that was directed against this calculation. In his thought experiment, 225 million Americans toss a coin every morning, and anyone who calls it wrong drops out. After twenty rounds, 225,000,000 ÷ 2²⁰ ≈ 215 winners remain, who consider themselves geniuses and write books. Buffett anticipated the objection that 225 million orangutans would arrive at the same result. But if 40 of the 215 winning orangutans came from the same zoo in Omaha, you would ask the zookeeper what he was feeding them. He saw such a cluster among nine investors whom he presented. All of them came from the school of Benjamin Graham, had completely different portfolios and yet all beat the market.

bloecke.titel: The superinvestors argument and the counterarguments
zeilen: The winners come from a group that could be identified in advance and not from a league table of top performers.
The group was described with hindsight in 1984. Investors from the same school who failed or gave up do not appear in the talk.
A list of candidates published before the start and left unchanged afterwards, with the results of all members.
Nine out of nine beat the index, and that is too many for chance.
Nine self-selected observations are not a test. The result depends on the selection rule.
The size of the population and the number of hits that pure chance would lead you to expect within it.
All followed the same method and bought below intrinsic value.
Today this method can be measured as a factor. In the USA, value delivered around 3.6% a year from 1926 to 2026, with no skill at all.
Whether any alpha remains after market, value, profitability and leverage.
The track records spanned ten to twenty years.
That is only enough with double-digit outperformance or a very calm style.
Calculate the t-value before talking about skill.

bloecke.md:
The third row of the table contains the strongest objection. What looked like a shared talent in 1984 has been a measurable characteristic since the work of Fama and French. From July 1926 to July 2026, the value factor delivered a geometric average of 3.59% a year in the USA, with t = 3.46, and no star manager is needed for that. At Berkshire, there is a second component that also has little to do with talent. The float of the insurance subsidiaries, $177.5 billion as of 30 June 2026, recently cost nothing and even brought in money. It acts as leverage that no retail fund can replicate. Frazzini, Kabiller and Pedersen attribute Berkshire's outperformance to this leverage and to a persistent tilt towards high-quality, low-volatility companies.

This does not prove that Buffett had no skill. But it shows that the 1984 talk was an argument and not a test. The more precisely you measure, the smaller the remainder that is left after style premiums, leverage and costs.

bloecke.md:
## League tables and chance

When enough candidates compete, winning streaks arise by themselves. Morningstar's European barometer covers around 32,000 funds domiciled in Europe. If each of these funds came out ahead in half of all years purely by chance, an average of 31 funds with an unbroken streak would remain after ten years. That would be 31 stories that sell well and contain no information whatsoever.

A second error of reasoning lies in the way streaks are counted. A streak measures how often someone was ahead, but not by how much. A manager who wins by a tenth of a point ten years in a row has a flawless record and yet an outperformance that hardly matters economically. Conversely, a manager with genuine outperformance can lag behind for several years in a row. The value factor itself returned minus 5.67% a year from January 2007 to December 2020.

Fund ratings and awards assess the past, usually over three to five years and on a risk-adjusted basis. For such periods, the calculation above provides no reliable conclusion. According to the U.S. Persistence Scorecard for year-end 2025, of the US equity funds that were in the top quarter of their category in 2021, none was back in the top quarter in each of the four following years, except among small caps (around 2%). Pure chance would give 0.25⁴ = 0.39%. Overall, the measured persistence is therefore even below the chance level.

bloecke.titel: Informative value of a track record
bloecke.unter: Only the top-right field, with a long track record and large outperformance, allows any conclusion at all, and almost no managers are found there.

felder.text: One point of outperformance over 20 years stays below t = 1 with normal dispersion. Even after two decades, the question remains undecided.
Statistically provable. But after deducting leverage, style premiums and fees, less remains than the headline suggests.
This is where the vast majority of any fund league table sits. The order changes every year without anything having changed.
Short track record, very large outperformance. This combination arises most easily by chance and is bought at the highest price.

bloecke.md:
## Requirements in German practice

The rules take the problem into account but do not solve it. Under Article 44(4) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565, past performance must not be the most prominent feature of marketing material; it must cover at least five years in twelve-month periods and carry a warning. The warning is correct. It protects against exaggeration, but not against mistaking random fluctuations for skill, because statistically five years are almost nothing.

The situation is similar for performance-related remuneration. Section 162(2) KAGB (German Investment Code) requires a performance fee to be described precisely in the fund's investment terms. The ESMA guidelines adopted by BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority) prescribe a reference period of at least five years so that earlier underperformance does not simply lapse. This period, too, is far shorter than what proof of skill requires.

An equity fund in the portfolio has built up a price gain of €10,000, and the money is to be switched in line with the new annual league table. The gain from the sale is investment income under Section 16(1) no. 3 in conjunction with Section 19 InvStG (Investment Tax Act). Equity funds receive a 30% partial exemption (Teilfreistellung, Section 20(1) InvStG), so €7,000 remains taxable. This is subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus a 5.5% solidarity surcharge on the tax, together 26.375%:

7,000 × 0.26375 = €1,846

The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) under Section 20(9) EStG (Income Tax Act) is not taken into account here. Which units count as sold first is determined by the FIFO rule of Section 20(4) EStG. The new fund starts with €1,846 less capital. If this is repeated every year, a selection determined by chance is set against a certain tax burden.

The threshold t = 2 applies to a single test specified in advance. If many candidates are tested at the same time, it is no longer usable. Of 1,000 managers with no skill at all, around 23 reach a t-value above 2 by chance alone, and just as many a value below minus 2. Together, this corresponds to the definition of a 5% level. Around one in 1,000 still lies above t = 3.

Harvey, Liu and Zhu made this argument for return factors in 2016. Hou, Xue and Zhang re-examined 447 anomalies. Of these, 64% did not even pass the threshold t = 1.96, and at t = 3, 85% failed. A search for conspicuous patterns among 32,000 funds is certain to find some. The only open question then is whether the search criterion was set beforehand or afterwards.

mitnehmen: Every result is made up of skill and chance, and the two can never be separated on the basis of the result alone, only weighed against each other.
Using t = (outperformance ÷ tracking error) × √(years), three points of outperformance with an 8% tracking error need 28 years to reach t = 2.
The more evenly skill is distributed, the more luck decides the ranking, which is known as the paradox of skill.
Buffett's superinvestors talk is a strong argument but not a statistical test, because the group was drawn up after the fact and the shared method is available today as a low-cost factor premium.
Before outperformance counts as skill, style premiums, leverage and costs have to be deducted, and it must be established who selected the candidate and when.

begriffe.text: The higher and more even the skill of all participants, the more strongly chance determines the ranking. The observed dispersion consists of skill and chance. If the share of skill becomes smaller, chance predominates.

Standard deviation of the return difference between a portfolio and its benchmark, stated in percentage points a year. It is the denominator in the significance calculation. The larger it is, the longer a track record has to be to prove anything.

Outperformance relative to the benchmark divided by the tracking error. Values around 0.5 are considered very good. The t-value of a track record is the information ratio times the square root of the years.

Measure of how many standard errors a measured value lies away from zero. From about 2, a single test is regarded as significant. When many candidates are tested at the same time, Harvey, Liu and Zhu call for at least 3.
